newsitem.title: RWANDA: Shooting shows Tutsi rebels meeting resistance.
newsitem.headline: Shooting shows Tutsi rebels meeting resistance.

text.p: Gunfire showed Tutsi rebels met some resistance on Sunday in a lightning offensive in eastern Zaire despite support from Rwandan troops in the city of Goma.

As international concern grew about the fate of more than a million refugees and Zaireans abandoned in eastern Zaire, France took the lead in urging its European partners to be prepared to intervene in an attempt to head off a disaster in the region.
From the rebel-held eastern Zairean city of Bukavu, Reuters photographer Corinne Dufka reported hearing 15 heavy explosions for about 90 minutes on Sunday from the north towards the city airport.

She quoted a Bukavu resident as saying they saw smoke coming from four Rwandan refugee camps near the airport and said most of the battle-hardened rebel elite had pulled out from the town towards the frontlines.
Sporadic gunfire in Goma city centre and around its airport, a key target five km (three miles) to the north, could be heard in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi overnight and on Sunday.
"We're very short of bandages, medicine and food for the patients. If the fighting starts again it will be disastrous," said Zairean doctor Albert Wasso at Bukavu General Hospital.
Some 40 patients, all with gunshot wounds, lay in the hospital, which has only Wasso and a few nurses and no surgeon.

In the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi, troops of the Rwanda Patriotic Army (RPA) stopped journalists from reaching Goma and Rwanda played down any RPA role in fighting pitting Zairean troops and exiled Rwandan Hutu militiamen against Tutsi rebels.

"We have categorically no intention of formally, militarily going in to Zaire. I don't believe anybody from the RPA is going there," said Rwandan Defence Ministry spokesman Emmanuel Ndahiro in Gisenyi.
"I am having discussions with (Rwandan) military authorities in Gisenyi and if we discover they were RPA (in Goma) we will treat them as individual, undisciplined cases," he told Reuters.

Witnesses however said RPA troops thrust into Goma by boat across Lake Kivu and by land on Friday. RPA reinforcements took Reuters journalists with them into Goma on Saturday and fought Zairean troops, who had lost control over much of the city.
More than a million refugees in eastern Zaire were left to their fate on Saturday with the evacuation by road of more than 100 international aid workers from Goma after a string of rebel victories.

International efforts to help them were largely on hold on Sunday with aid agencies trying to contact the rebels to allow staff into rebel-held areas of eastern Zaire and very little news filtering out from the war zone on refugee movements.
Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said some of the estimated 400,000 people crammed into Mugunga camp were moving westwards along the shores of Lake Kivu.

"It is likely these people were panicked into fleeing by the fighting, which appears to be moving westwards," he added. Mugunga is now the world's largest refugee camp and is a centre of concerns about possible epidemics spread by poor sanitation.
Aid officials say they fear tens of thousands may die of hunger and disease in the war zone unless help reaches them.
A French cabinet member called on France's European partners on Sunday to be prepared to intervene to prevent a human disaster in Zaire but warned that France could not act alone.
"We (France) are already pre-positioning supplies, food, water, shelters and clothing," Secretary of State for emergency humanitarian action Xavier Emmanuelli told TF-1 television.
Officials said the French government was waiting to see whether African heads of state who meet on the Zaire fighting in Nairobi on Tuesday, call for action by the European Union.
The Zairean government however has said it will not attend the Nairobi talks as long as Rwanda troops occupy its territory.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, called for the immediate opening of emergency lifelines to the masses fleeing to some of the most inhospitable areas of Zaire.
"This may be a final appeal to all those involved in this terrible conflict, or it will be too late," she said.
In the Zairean capital Kinshasa, mobs looted and burned property belonging to Tutsis at the weekend amid growing signs of a witchhunt in response to the Tutsi revolt in the east.
Ethnic Tutsis, who prior to the conflict featured prominently in Zaire's business and professional communities, were packing up and trying to leave the city.
An Organisation of African Unity (OAU) peace mission arrived in Rwanda from Zaire on Sunday and Rwanda's president visited Uganda as diplomatic activity over the fighting stepped up.
Diplomats in Kigali however were sceptical about chances of success for the OAU, saying it lacked the political muscle to bring the warring sides in Zaire to the negotiating table.
